jensen:sH5qyeHSdVs.title: Nvidia’s CEO on the AI debt scare, China, and jobs | Full interview
jensen:sH5qyeHSdVs.snippet: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang came straight off the GTC Berlin stage to take the question rattling the AI trade: can the neoclouds pay ...
jensen:sH5qyeHSdVs.desc:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang came straight off the GTC Berlin stage to take the question rattling the AI trade: can the neoclouds pay for all this? Huang told veteran business journalist Deirdre Bosa that the answer is the chips themselves.

He says Nvidia GPUs stay productive for seven or eight years, not four, which makes them collateral a lender can underwrite. "Nobody gives a credit for that," he says. Nvidia has a stake in that argument, since it guarantees part of its chips' resale value on some financed projects.

He also explains why he thinks the AI jobs narrative is "precisely wrong" and why nobody manufactures AI researchers at scale like China.

Featuring
Jensen Huang, Founder and Chief Executive Officer, NVIDIA
Deirdre Bosa
Gavin Baker, Managing Partner and Chief Investment Officer, Atreides Management

The path there, Jensen says, is building your own "super agents": domain-specific systems wrapped in an open harness, grounded in your data, and improved over time. NVIDIA and LangChain also announce a new blueprint for running Deep Agents with Nemotron 3 Ultra inside OpenShell, a secure, open runtime, giving every enterprise the building blocks to create and deploy super agents anywhere.

We also discuss:
• Why companies of the future are built on harnesses, not business processes
• The difference between open vs. frontier models
• How Nemotron 3 Ultra reaches near-frontier performance at a low cost
• Why cheaper, faster intelligence finds better answers
• When to start with frontier models and when to specialize
• Why more AI means more jobs

jensen:2UpQbeAZuqA.title: NVIDIA's Jensen Huang on Building the Dynamo of the Intelligence Age
jensen:2UpQbeAZuqA.snippet: Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA, makes the case that computing is undergoing its biggest shift in 60 years: from ...
jensen:2UpQbeAZuqA.desc:
Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA, makes the case that computing is undergoing its biggest shift in 60 years: from retrieval, where data centers store files we look up, to generation, where every word, image, and video is produced in real time and customized for whoever is asking. He explains why NVIDIA's AI factories are the dynamos of this era: machines that take in electrons and send out tokens of intelligence, just as Siemens' dynamo once turned motion into electricity. Jensen frames intelligence as the third force to "cocoon" the planet after electricity and the internet. He describes the five-layer cake of AI investment—energy, chips, infrastructure, models, applications—and dismantles the fear that AI will erase jobs, using radiology and software engineering to show how automation raised labor demand instead of killing it. His bottom line: you won't lose your job to AI, but you might lose it to someone who uses AI.

Hosted by Konstantine Buhler, Sequoia Capital 
Recorded May, 2026

lisasu:-sKAMB10eh0.snippet: AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su reflects on the experiences that shaped her career as an engineer and technology leader, from ...
lisasu:-sKAMB10eh0.desc:
AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su reflects on the experiences that shaped her career as an engineer and technology leader, from growing up in New York and discovering an early curiosity about how things work to building a career in the semiconductor industry and ultimately leading AMD.

In this NYSE Live conversation, Su discusses the importance of building technology and products that make an impact. She recalls her early experiences with semiconductors, her time at Texas Instruments and IBM, and the career advice that encouraged her to “run towards the hardest problems.” Su explains how taking on difficult challenges, volunteering for important projects, and being willing to learn helped shape her approach to leadership.

She also discusses joining AMD, taking on the CEO role, and approaching the company’s challenges with a long-term mindset. Su explains that major decisions in technology can take years to deliver results and shares why she believed AMD could build high-performance technology capable of making a difference.

Turning to artificial intelligence, Su describes herself as an “AI optimist” and calls AI the most powerful technology she has seen during her more than 30 years in technology. At the same time, she emphasizes the importance of AI safety, safeguards, industry collaboration, and building trust as AI technology continues to advance.

Dr. Su holds bachelor’s, master’s and PhD degrees in electrical engineering from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. She is an IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) fellow, and a member of the National Academy of Engineering and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.  

Time magazine named Dr. Su its 2024 CEO of the Year, and she has received the Global Semiconductor Alliance’s Dr. Morris Chang Exemplary Leadership Award and the Semiconductor Industry Association’s Robert N. Noyce Award. She serves as chair of the board of directors of the Semiconductor Industry Association.

lisasu:aHdOqHqtcQI.snippet: In a live discussion at Bloomberg Tech in Las Vegas, AMD CEO Lisa Su speaks with Bloomberg Tech Co-Host Ed Ludlow about ...
lisasu:aHdOqHqtcQI.desc:
In a live discussion at Bloomberg Tech in Las Vegas, AMD CEO Lisa Su speaks with Bloomberg Tech Co-Host Ed Ludlow about the company's current customer base and demand, partnerships and compute capacity, and more. Su says that AI is "not hype," adding that she anticipates global demand will balloon to 5 billion users over the next several years. Su also discusses demand in the Chinese market for AMD's broad range of chips.

 Advanced Micro Devices Inc., aiming to make a dent in Nvidia Corp.’s stranglehold on the AI hardware market, announced a new chip for corporate data center use and talked up the attributes of a future generation of products for that market.
The company is adding a new model to its current lineup – one called the MI440X – for use in smaller corporate data centers where customers can deploy local hardware and keep data inside their own facilities. The announcement came as part of a keynote at the CES trade show, where Chief Executive Officer Lisa Su also touted AMD’s top-of-the-line MI455X, saying systems based on that chip are a leap forward in the capabilities on offer.
Su also added her voice to a chorus of US tech executives, including her counterpart at Nvidia, arguing that the AI surge will continue because of the benefits it’s bringing and the heavy computing requirements of that new technology.
“We don’t have nearly enough compute for what we could possibly do,” Su said. “The rate and pace of AI innovation has been incredible over the last few years.

lipbutan:Nz2e-RJdRso.snippet: "Before you retire, save Intel." That's the phrase that pulled Lip-Bu Tan back in — but this conversation is about everything that ...
lipbutan:Nz2e-RJdRso.desc:
"Before you retire, save Intel." That's the phrase that pulled Lip-Bu Tan back in — but this conversation is about everything that came before it.

In this episode of A Bit Personal, Jodi Shelton sits down with Lip-Bu Tan, CEO of Intel, to talk about the life behind the title. Lip-Bu started out studying physics and nuclear engineering, then spent decades as one of the semiconductor industry's most active investors, backing hundreds of companies and helping build the venture ecosystem that powers today's tech world. Even now, leading one of the most iconic names in American technology, he still runs his own venture funds — a rare dual life that shapes how he thinks about long-term bets, talent, and building things that last.

We talk about the mentors and moments that shaped his instincts as both an investor and a leader, how he thinks about speed, culture, and people inside a company as large and storied as Intel, and what continues to energize him after four decades in the industry. Lip-Bu opens up about what leadership actually feels like day to day, not just from the outside looking in.
This is a conversation about curiosity, conviction, and what it looks like to lead with both a founder's instincts and an investor's patience.

lipbutan:asCgCv2XB4s.desc:
At 66 years old, instead of heading towards retirement, former Cadence CEO and legendary investor Lip Bu Tan decided to take on the hardest job in tech: turning Intel around. Elad Gil and Sarah Guo sit down with Intel CEO Lip Bu Tan to talk about why he took the job and what “saving” Intel actually looks like. Tan explains how his experience in startup culture informed his decisions to drive Intel’s culture towards faster decisions, focus on customer satisfaction, and engineer accountability. He also discusses his strategy to strengthen Intel’s balance sheet by welcoming investments from Jensen Huang’s Nvidia, Softbank, and the US government. Tan also shares his product roadmap that centers the CPU for agentic AI and inference, the collaboration with Elon Musk on Terafab, his investing framework for semiconductors, and his views on how AI is reshaping design and operations at, as he puts it, a ‘legacy spreadsheet’ tech company.

lipbutan:FtxWTNaUXkc.snippet: Lip-Bu Tan has spent decades near the center of Silicon Valley's hardware cycles. He started out as a contrarian semiconductor ...
lipbutan:FtxWTNaUXkc.desc:
Lip-Bu Tan has spent decades near the center of Silicon Valley's hardware cycles. He started out as a contrarian semiconductor investor when the category was out of favor, then as the CEO who turned around Cadence Design Systems over 15 years, and now as CEO of Intel. In this episode of TechSurge, host Michael Marks sits down with his longtime friend Lip-Bu Tan for a personal, wide-ranging conversation rather than a standard interview.

Tan discusses his path from Malaysia and MIT nuclear engineering to Silicon Valley, his early conviction in semiconductors as an investor when venture capital had moved on to software, and the origins of his bets on SambaNova, Cerebras, and other companies now central to the AI compute buildout. He shared the lessons of turning around Cadence as a first-time CEO and how that same customer-focused, listening-first culture applies to a much larger and more complex challenge at Intel, one that spans both chip design and foundry manufacturing. The conversation covers Intel's vertical integration strategy, the push to rebuild CPU leadership for the agentic AI era, high-speed connectivity and photonics investments, advanced packaging and cooling, and a look at memory architecture as a renewed area of focus. The episode closes on the personal side of competing with old friends across the industry.

The conversation covers:
- Intel's roadmap for the next decade
- Why AI's future extends beyond GPUs
- Semiconductors, packaging, photonics and memory

feifei:5Q4804-uwtY.snippet: Fei-Fei Li taught machines to see. Now she's asking which human traits they can't replace. | Subscribe to Futurology!
feifei:5Q4804-uwtY.desc:
Fei-Fei Li taught machines to see. Now she’s asking which human traits they can’t replace.  | Subscribe to Futurology! https://linkin.bio/futurology/

The fears of what AI will do to us often come down to one word: replace. Our jobs. Our creativity. Our place atop the evolutionary totem pole. But that word assumes a very specific idea of what makes humans special, when really, that may have very little to do with the tasks we’re asking machines to replace us for.

In this episode, recorded in February 2025, AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li argues the word has to go. Li built ImageNet, the dataset that taught computers to recognize the world. Now at World Labs, she’s teaching them the space they move through, instead of flat pictures of it. And with her Human-Centered AI initiative at Stanford, she wants that capacity measured against three human outcomes: dignity, agency, and community. Anything that replaces or degrades those, she says, should be a non-starter.

feifei:Ctjiatnd6Xk.desc:
Dr. Fei-Fei Li is known as the “godmother of AI.” She’s been at the center of AI’s biggest breakthroughs for over two decades. She spearheaded ImageNet, the dataset that sparked the deep-learning revolution we’re living right now, served as Google Cloud’s Chief AI Scientist, directed Stanford’s Artificial Intelligence Lab, and co-founded Stanford’s Institute for Human-Centered AI. In this conversation, Fei-Fei shares the rarely told history of how we got here—including the wild fact that just nine years ago, calling yourself an AI company was basically a death sentence.

*We discuss:*
1. How ImageNet helped spark the AI explosion we’re living through
2. Why world models and spatial intelligence represent the next frontier in AI, beyond large language models
3. Why Fei-Fei believes AI won’t replace humans but will require us to take responsibility for ourselves
4. The surprising applications of Marble, from movie production to psychological research
5. Why robotics faces unique challenges compared with language models and what’s needed to overcome them
6. How to participate in AI regardless of your role

Fei-Fei Li and Justin Johnson are cofounders of World Labs, who have recently launched Marble (https://marble.worldlabs.ai/), a new kind of generative “world model” that can create editable 3D environments from text, images, and other spatial inputs. Marble lets creators generate persistent 3D worlds, precisely control cameras, and interactively edit scenes, making it a powerful tool for games, film, VR, robotics simulation, and more. In this episode, Fei-Fei and Justin share how their journey from ImageNet and Stanford research led to World Labs, why spatial intelligence is the next frontier after LLMs, and how world models could change how machines see, understand, and build in 3D.
We discuss:

* The massive compute scaling from AlexNet to today and why world models and spatial data are the most compelling way to “soak up” modern GPU clusters compared to language alone.
* What Marble actually is: a generative model of 3D worlds that turns text and images into editable scenes using Gaussian splats, supports precise camera control and recording, and runs interactively on phones, laptops, and VR headsets.
* Fei-fei’s essay (https://drfeifei.substack.com/p/from-words-to-worlds-spatial-intelligence) on *spatial intelligence* as a distinct form of intelligence from language: from picking up a mug to inferring the 3D structure of DNA, and why language is a lossy, low-bandwidth channel for describing the rich 3D/4D world we live in.

sundar:fJBSNEFdm8c.title: Sundar Pichai on what's next for Google Gemini, Waymo, and data centers in space
sundar:fJBSNEFdm8c.snippet: Even Google can't get enough compute. I sit down with Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai shortly after the wider release of ...
sundar:fJBSNEFdm8c.desc:
Even Google can’t get enough compute. I sit down with Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai shortly after the wider release of Gemini 4 Argon to discuss its early reception, where he still wants the model to improve, and what it takes to keep Google at the frontier of AI.

Pichai explains the recent leadership shakeup at Google DeepMind and why building frontier models has become an “all-consuming” job. We also get into Google’s answer to the personal agent race, how he predicts Gemini will do more work on your behalf, and whether agents will finally bring Search, Gmail, and Gemini together.

I ask him about Google turning free cash flow negative, the risks in the AI infrastructure buildout, and how he plans for demand years before knowing what the models will be capable of. He explains the signals giving him confidence to keep spending and how he uses AI agents to follow model development and compute usage inside Google.

We also discuss Project Suncatcher, Google’s new effort to put AI data centers in space, and why he thinks it belongs alongside bets like Waymo. He shares what’s next for Waymo and Wing, and when he expects quantum computing to become a real business.

sundar:RgV57kDzcng.desc:
When Sundar Pichai, Google’s chief executive, took the stage at Google I/O 2026, he outlined a vision of an A.I.-assisted future aimed at making life just a little bit easier in myriad ways.

This comes, however, against the backdrop of a growing public opinion problem for A.I. companies: graduates have booed mentions of artificial intelligence at commencements around the country, and a recent New York Times/Siena poll found that 35 percent of respondents viewed the technology as “mostly bad,” compared with just 16 percent who viewed it as “mostly good.”

After the I/O conference, Kevin Roose and Casey Newton, the hosts of "Hard Fork," sat down with Pichai to talk about Google’s place in the A.I. race, whether the usefulness of the company’s products will be enough to overcome public skepticism and what he expects for the future.

demis:DsewHeVbL-0.title: A Conversation with Demis Hassabis, Co-Founder and CEO of Google DeepMind
demis:DsewHeVbL-0.snippet: AI@GSB, the Dean's Applied AI initiative at the Stanford Graduate School of Business (GSB), and Stanford Medical School hosted ...
demis:DsewHeVbL-0.desc:
AI@GSB, the Dean's Applied AI initiative at the Stanford Graduate School of Business (GSB), and Stanford Medical School hosted a conversation with Demis Hassabis, Co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind, on the frontier of artificial intelligence and what it means for how we live, work, and flourish.

Introduced by GSB Dean Sarah Soule and moderated by Stanford President Jonathan Levin, the discussion ranged from the science behind today's AI breakthroughs, the path toward more general intelligence, and the responsibilities that come with building technology of this scale. Hassabis reflected on AlphaFold and AI's accelerating role in scientific discovery, the design choices that shape whether these systems serve human ends, and the questions leaders should be asking now.

The conversation extended a theme at the heart of Professor Jennifer Aaker's course, Designing AI for Human Flourishing — the idea that the measure of these technologies is not only what they can do, but whether they help people live fuller, more meaningful, more connected lives. Hassabis stressed the importance of the decisions we make over the next couple of years in determining these outcomes and that the future is not yet written.

In our final episode of the season, Professor Hannah Fry sits down with Google DeepMind Co-founder and CEO Demis Hassabis for their annual check-in. Together, they look beyond the product launches to the scientific and technological questions that will define the next decade.

Demis shares his vision for the path to AGI - from solving "root node" problems in fusion energy and material science to the rise of world models and simulations. They also explore what's beyond the frontier and the importance of balancing scientific rigor amid the competitive dynamics of AI advancement.

demis:JNyuX1zoOgU.title: Demis Hassabis: Agents, AGI & The Next Big Scientific Breakthrough
demis:JNyuX1zoOgU.snippet: Demis Hassabis has had one of the most extraordinary careers in tech. He started as a chess prodigy and video game designer at ...
demis:JNyuX1zoOgU.desc:
Demis Hassabis has had one of the most extraordinary careers in tech. He started as a chess prodigy and video game designer at 17 before getting a PhD in neuroscience and going on to found DeepMind. His lab cracked Go, solved protein structure prediction with AlphaFold, and then gave it away free to every scientist on earth. That work won him the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Today he leads Google DeepMind, pushing toward the same goal he set as a teenager: AGI. 

On this special live episode of How to Build the Future, he sat down with YC's Garry Tan to talk about what still needs to happen to get us to AGI, his advice for founders on how to stay ahead of the curve and what the next big scientific breakthroughs might be.

He solved “the most important unsolved problem in science”… 
If you need more optimistic science and tech stories, subscribe to support HUGE*!

Demis Hassabis is a Nobel Prize winner and CEO of Google DeepMind. He is one of the most important people alive on what is quickly becoming the biggest technological advance of our lifetime. Because the biggest way AI is going to impact your life, you can’t see. 

It’s not a chatbot or an image generator. It’s the tools he and his team are building that are invisible to you – in new drug design, nuclear fusion, natural disasters detection, quantum computers. 

So who Demis is and what he chooses to build matters a lot. And he’s fascinating… 

He’s a childhood chess prodigy who at 17 turned down a reportedly million dollar job offer from a gaming company to go to college instead, and then get a PhD in neuroscience. He founded his company DeepMind with a mission to “solve intelligence” – starting with beating video games. He sold that company to Google specifically because they promised to let DeepMind focus on scientific research.

But as this has turned into the most intense technological battle in recent history, Demis is now in charge of much much more. He’s now behind basically everything Google does in AI.

He’s making decisions that affect your life and millions of other lives every single day.

So what is he planning to do with all that power?

demis:AFpeWo1GTeg.desc:
Demis Hassabis, co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind and 2024 Nobel laureate in chemistry for AlphaFold, joins Sequoia partner Konstantine Buhler at AI Ascent 2026 for a wide-ranging conversation about the path to AGI and what comes after. He explains why he believes AGI is achievable by 2030, why drug discovery could collapse from ten years to days, and why we should think of information, not matter or energy, as the most fundamental substance in the universe. Also: what Einstein would tell us about the limits of today's models, and why the next year or two will be critical for humanity.

demis:hV-CkdC8B7I.title: Demis Hassabis on Accelerating Scientific Discovery With AI
demis:hV-CkdC8B7I.snippet: Sir Demis Hassabis delivers the lecture "Accelerating Scientific Discovery with AI" during a March 2025 visit to the University of ...
demis:hV-CkdC8B7I.desc:
Sir Demis Hassabis delivers the lecture "Accelerating Scientific Discovery with AI" during a March 2025 visit to the University of Cambridge, hosted by the Department of Computer Science and Technology.

The lecture sets out his long running argument that the route to broad scientific progress runs through building general purpose artificial intelligence first, then applying it to hard scientific problems. He traces the work from game playing systems including AlphaGo, through AlphaFold's prediction of protein structures, to the use of AI as a discovery tool across biology and chemistry, including the drug design work spun out into Isomorphic Labs.

Hassabis is co-founder and chief executive of Google DeepMind, founded in London, and shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with John Jumper for AlphaFold. He is a UK government AI adviser and was educated at Cambridge and University College London.

The material speaks directly to the question of how UK research capability converts into economic and scientific output, which other content on this channel addresses from the funding and policy side.
Source: Cambridge Department of Computer Science and Technology.

demis:hb9JPW_DkpQ.title: DeepMind Chief Demis Hassabis Says Google’s Still Winning AI Talent | Semafor Tech
demis:hb9JPW_DkpQ.snippet: Following a string of departures among its top AI leaders, @googledeepmind CEO Demis Hassabis dismissed the notion that ...
demis:hb9JPW_DkpQ.desc:
Following a string of departures among its top AI leaders, @googledeepmind CEO Demis Hassabis dismissed the notion that Google was losing its grip on leading AI talent and said he remains confident in the company’s ability to attract and retain the best people.

Even as well-funded rivals and nimble startups poach its top brass, “we have by far the biggest and broadest research bench of any of the labs out there,” Hassabis told Semafor Tech Editor Reed Albergotti during an on-stage interview at the Cannes Lions Festival. “We win our fair share of the top talent.”

Google’s shares tumbled as much as 7% on Monday following the exits of top AI thinkers Noam Shazeer and John Jumper, which sparked anxiety on Wall Street over Google’s ability to retain talent as the battle for AI minds escalates from a Silicon Valley sub-plot to a central focus for global investors.

“There’s a lot of talent movement between all the leading labs,” Hassabis noted, chalking it up to the most “ferociously competitive” job market the tech industry has ever seen.

I sat down with Dario Amodei in Bangalore. He built Claude, but he started as a biologist looking for a tool to cure disease. Today, he's at the helm of an AI revolution that he compares to a tsunami society is actively ignoring. We got into the heavy stuff: why Anthropic secretly withheld a working model before ChatGPT existed, whether AI is on the verge of consciousness, and if outsourcing our thinking is going to make humans measurably stupider. Dario makes the case that coding is a dying skill, critical thinking is our last real edge, and the absurd concentration of power in AI right now is a massive problem, even though he’s one of the people holding it.

The siblings and co-founders of Claude AI, the CEO, Dario Amodei, and the President, Daniela Amodei, sit down with Oprah for an in-depth discussion on Artificial Intelligence and its profound impact on all of us.  Anthropic is one of the largest tech companies leading AI development including their enormously popular chatbot assistant Claude.  Dario and Daniela discuss the ethical responsibility and moral questions that come with creating advanced A.I., their new model Mythos and share their thoughts around government regulation. dario:OyAN7XsEUBY.desc:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is set to speak at Salesforce's Dreamforce Summit.  Amodei and other tech CEOS have recently split with the federal government on whether to slow AI development.
 
“If slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in a blog post on Sept. 12.
 
Both Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, agreed with Amodei in social media posts over the weekend.  
 
President Donald Trump has brushed aside the CEOs warnings, telling reporters at a golf tournament in Ireland, “We can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up and they're bringing up things that won't happen.”

altman:kG8AoExkX40.title: Sam Altman on Building OpenAI & Betting on the Impossible
altman:kG8AoExkX40.snippet: Sam Altman has spent his career at the intersection of startups, investing and artificial intelligence. He says he was fascinated by ...
altman:kG8AoExkX40.desc:
Sam Altman has spent his career at the intersection of startups, investing and artificial intelligence. He says he was fascinated by AI as a child in St. Louis, studied it in college and eventually helped start OpenAI in 2015 after concluding that the most important opportunities often begin as non-consensus bets. His experience investing in startups taught him to look for power laws, back unconventional talent and recognize the decisions that can change a company’s trajectory.

At OpenAI, Altman says most of his effort goes toward research and compute. Scaling compute requires coordinating chips, fabrication plants, data centers, power systems, finance, policy, supply chains and logistics—what he describes as potentially the most expensive infrastructure project in history. He argues OpenAI should function primarily as a platform: one direct interface to powerful AI and one application programming interface that lets people build on top of it. That strategy requires killing good ideas to preserve resources for the great ones.

Altman expects AI capabilities to advance faster than society and the economy can absorb them. Human habits and institutional inertia will slow the transition, which he believes may make it smoother. He also expects human connection to become more valuable and AI to enable a major increase in small-business formation. His central concern is that AI should expand human agency rather than concentrate power in a small number of companies, people or models

zuck:XNOuhxUsQDI.title: Mark Zuckerberg's Plan for a Personal AI That Works For You | Meet Muse
zuck:XNOuhxUsQDI.snippet: Mark Zuckerberg joins me to introduce Muse, Meta's new personal AI agent, and explain why trust and safety are the whole make ...
zuck:XNOuhxUsQDI.desc:
Mark Zuckerberg joins me to introduce Muse, Meta's new personal AI agent, and explain why trust and safety are the whole make or break for personal superintelligence.

In this interview, Zuckerberg shares how he actually uses Muse: running standing weekend baking projects with his daughter, planning multi-week robot builds, snagging hard-to-get mountain climbing permits, and even getting coached between MMA rounds by cameras in his gym. He explains the vision of personal superintelligence for everyone, the free tier (100 million tokens a week), and the security architecture behind it all, including the confidential VM designed so that even Meta can't see inside, a secure credential vault, one-time virtual cards for payments, and a second "sentinel" agent that keeps yours in check.

Why Muse is a big deal: it's Meta's first consumer personal agent that doesn't just answer questions, it does the work. It sets its own projects through an Ideas feed, remembers your life with nightly memory compaction, and asks permission before touching anything sensitive. If agents are the next platform shift, this is Meta's bid to put one in billions of people's hands, free.

zuck:u8cYwaLzN-k.desc:
Biohub started with an ambitious goal of curing, preventing, and managing all disease by the end of the century. A decade later, thanks to the convergence of frontier AI and biological data, that goal may have been too conservative. In this episode, Elad Gil and Sarah Guo sit down with Biohub co-founders Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan, alongside Biohub Head of Science Alex Rives. Together, they discuss Biohub’s $500 million virtual biology initiative, which integrates frontier AI with wet-lab work to build predictive world models of cells, proteins, and systems. They also talk about their newly announced open-source engine for digital protein and antibody design, ESMFold2; why Biohub is a nonprofit rather than a venture-backed startup; and how hierarchical simulations will soon allow doctors to treat patients at an individual, mechanistic level.

Priscilla Chan and Mark Zuckerberg join a16z’s Ben Horowitz, Erik Torenberg, and Vineeta Agarwala to share how the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative is building the computational tools that will accelerate the cure, prevention, and management of all disease by century's end.

They explain why basic science needs $100 million-scale projects that traditional NIH grants can't fund, how their Cell Atlas became biology's missing periodic table with millions of cells catalogued in open-source format, and why their new virtual cell models will let scientists test high-risk hypotheses in silico before investing in expensive wet lab work.

Plus: the organizational shift unifying the Biohub under AI leadership, what happens when biologists and engineers sit side-by-side, and why modern biology labs are expanding compute instead of square footage.

satya:CUgS4y4XiNY.snippet: Four years on from the launch of ChatGPT, AI's impact on the world — outside of software development — has been incremental, ...
satya:CUgS4y4XiNY.desc:
Four years on from the launch of ChatGPT, AI’s impact on the world — outside of software development — has been incremental, not exponential. And Microsoft is less about making competitors like Google dance than it is about getting down to the nitty gritty of making AI work predictably and reliably. At Microsoft’s CISO summit, Reed sat down with Satya Nadella, who has gone back to being the CEO of a company that is building a sturdy dance floor.

“We, as an industry, have to wake up to this,” Nadella said. “It’s not about the shiny object and FOMO.”

They also discuss whether “superintelligence” is a good rebrand, whether alignment is still possible, and if the 59-year-old Microsoft CEO has started thinking about succession.

satya:giE1O1-e2DY.title: Satya Nadella on the AI backlash, and the rise of agents
satya:giE1O1-e2DY.snippet: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella thinks AI agents will create a market “orders of magnitude” bigger than the cloud. I sat down with him ...
satya:giE1O1-e2DY.desc:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella thinks AI agents will create a market “orders of magnitude” bigger than the cloud.

I sat down with him at Microsoft’s recent customer event in Seattle for the unveiling of the new Copilot. We discuss Autopilot, its new, OpenClaw-based agent that can work on your behalf, and why he thinks newer AI models are finally capable of delivering on more of Copilot’s promise.

Nadella also has a blunt assessment of the AI industry: “We are way too self-obsessed.” I ask him why the industry has struggled to explain its benefits and what it will take to earn people’s trust.

We get into his concerns about agents acting deceptively, when a safety problem should stop a release, and why he doesn’t want AI oversight to become a “cartel-like arrangement.”

We also discuss Microsoft’s relationship with OpenAI, the models Microsoft is building itself, and why Nadella wants investors to think about its apps, agents, and infrastructure as one connected business. He explains how he uses AI to track Microsoft’s capital spending, shares his vision for “unmetered intelligence” on Windows, and gives an update on Xbox’s path back to growth.

satya:2fD2HXr9HXo.title: Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella on Empathy and Lessons He Learned the Hard Way
satya:2fD2HXr9HXo.snippet: Ali sits with Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella who reflects on growing up in Hyderabad, India with academically ...
satya:2fD2HXr9HXo.desc:
Ali sits with Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella who reflects on growing up in Hyderabad, India with academically accomplished parents, his early obsession with cricket, and a lifelong focus on getting a little better each year. He describes standing up to bullies, being introduced to computing through a Sinclair ZX80, working at Sun, and joining Microsoft in 1992.

Satya shares formative lessons about empathy, including an interview moment where he was told to hypothetically “pick up and hug” a fallen child, and how his late son Zain’s cerebral palsy reshaped his perspective on leadership. He regrets early management failures, discusses missed strategic opportunities around search and keyword auctions in the search wars, and emphasizes courage, persistence, and taking risks while empowering others.

satya:BKx0Dp8y-6g.snippet: Reid sits down with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella fresh off Microsoft Build 2026. The conversation goes wide: how AI is reshaping ...
satya:BKx0Dp8y-6g.desc:
Reid sits down with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella fresh off Microsoft Build 2026. The conversation goes wide: how AI is reshaping work, business, and society—and why the transformation sweeping through software development today is only a preview of what's coming for all knowledge work. Satya makes the case that human capital and "token capital" are now deeply intertwined, that companies—not just countries—must build their own AI capabilities, and that the organizations best positioned to thrive are those that can leverage their unique expertise inside intelligent systems. Reid and Satya also explore Microsoft's enterprise AI vision, Reid's work with Manas on AI-powered scientific discovery, lessons from past technological revolutions, and why demonstrating real, tangible benefits may be the most important thing the industry can do to earn—and keep—the public's trust.

satya:VbskphfI5Yo.title: All-In Podcast Live with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella | USA House
satya:VbskphfI5Yo.snippet: A fireside chat between Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and AI & Crypto Czar David Sacks, recorded live at USA House Davos 2026 ...
satya:VbskphfI5Yo.desc:
A fireside chat between Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and AI & Crypto Czar David Sacks, recorded live at USA House Davos 2026, and it covered a lot of ground fast.

Nadella opened with the story almost nobody knows: arriving in the U.S. for grad school, earning his green card, then voluntarily giving it up and returning to the American embassy in Delhi to get an H1 visa so his wife could join him. There was, he noted, no line for giving up a green card.

From there the conversation moved to the central question of the AI moment for enterprise: what does it actually mean for a knowledge worker to use these tools, and where is Microsoft taking Copilot? Nadella traced the arc from autocomplete to chat to actions to fully autonomous agents, and argued the question is not cloud versus edge, it is how all these form factors compose. His preferred metaphor for the AI age, borrowed from the CEO of Notion: a manager of infinite minds, macro-delegating while micro-steering agents running in parallel.

On enterprise adoption, Nadella's view is that it is both top-down and bottom-up simultaneously, the way PCs spread through companies in the 1980s: lawyers brought in Word, finance brought in Excel, email became standard issue. Today the equivalent is teams building agents to remove drudgery from their workflows, one at a time. In this 20-minute technical lecture, AI pioneer Ilya Sutskever breaks down the foundational architecture of modern large language models, the looming walls of the pure pre-training paradigm, and why agentic systems represent the critical next frontier for artificial intelligence.

From the core mechanics of autoregressive next-token prediction to biological scaling analogies and the rise of inference-time compute, this talk provides a masterclass on where AI has been and where it is heading.

9:00 – The Next Paradigm: Agents, Synthetic Data & Inference-Time Compute

11:30 – Biological Scaling Analogy (Brain-to-Body Exponents)

14:00 – Superintelligence, Reasoning & Deliberative Systems

17:30 – Closing Remarks & Final Reflections

The Post-Pre-Training Era: Analyzing data scarcity constraints and why raw scale alone is hitting natural boundaries.

Agentic Workflows: Moving past static prompting and context windows toward structured, goal-directed systems with feedback mechanisms.

Inference-Time Compute: How allocating more compute during inference unlocks deeper reasoning and qualitative shifts in capability.

karpathy:96jN2OCOfLs.desc:
Andrej Karpathy (co-founder of OpenAI, former head of AI at Tesla, and now founder of Eureka Labs) talks with Sequoia partner Stephanie Zhan at AI Ascent 2026 about what's changed in the year since he coined "vibe coding." He explains why he's never felt more behind as a programmer, why agentic engineering is the more serious discipline taking shape on top of vibe coding, and why we should think of LLMs not as animals but as ghosts: jagged, statistical, summoned entities that require a new kind of taste and judgment to direct. He also touches on Software 3.0, the limits of verifiability, and why you can outsource your thinking but never your understanding.

karpathy:Rlk0GLRWwTI.desc:
Andrej Karpathy and AI systems engineering into a single hour.

His core thesis: "You can actually delete everything… Delete everything, keep Graph."

Here is the entire roadmap broken down:

1. The Foundation (10%): Treat the LLM as a raw computer you reprogram on the fly.
2. The Code (30%): Natural language is your new programming syntax.
3. The Agency (50%): Connect memory, tools, and context so predictions trigger execution.
4. The Loops (70%): Keep inference-time reasoning strictly separate from weight optimization.
5. The Network (100%): Turn complex agent workflows into directed, message-passing graphs.

jensen:ZEL0EAVtCTY.desc:
Today, NVIDIA is widely recognized as one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. But when founder and CEO Jensen Huang set out to build the company more than three decades ago, it was considered an extraordinarily risky bet on a new approach to computing. How did Huang, an immigrant from working-class roots in Taiwan, build NVIDIA into a company at the center of the AI revolution, and could he have done so anywhere other than the United States?

In this episode of Only in America, Condoleezza Rice sits down with Huang at NVIDIA’s Silicon Valley headquarters to explore the experiences, opportunities, and institutions that shaped his remarkable journey. Huang reflects on coming to America as a child, the culture of ambition and innovation that influenced him, the vision that led him to found NVIDIA, and the perseverance required to navigate years of uncertainty and skepticism.

Today, the CEO of Google gives a rare interview to discuss AI, economic risk, climate change and much more.

BBC economics editor Faisal Islam has been speaking to Sundar Pichai, the head of Google’s parent company Alphabet, about the future of the AI bubble.

The tech boss warned that “no company is going to be immune” if the AI bubble bursts after its current period of boom. This comes as some analysts expressed fear that stock markets are heading for a repeat of the dotcom bubble burst of the late 1990s.

They also discussed the environmental cost of powering AI, the potential risks to jobs and whether the UK will benefit from the current boom. BBC economics editor Faisal Islam joins Adam in the studio.

Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis expresses surprise that OpenAI moved to ads “so early,” while noting that Google has no current plans to put them in Gemini. We talked about what’s coming for Gemini, the new Apple partnership that will put Gemini behind Siri, competing with OpenAI, and what he believes is missing on the road to AGI. We also discussed the return of Google Glass, how he thinks the robotics market will develop, his views on brain-computer interfaces, and his timeline for AGI. As you’ll be able to tell, Hassabis is feeling confident about Google’s position in the AI race. At the same time, he’s more conservative about AI’s rate of progress than some of his peers.

altman:iKFqJOSWHTE.title: Sam Altman on Elon Musk, ‘Artificial,’ and the Future of Humanity (Part One)
altman:iKFqJOSWHTE.snippet: Every day a new scientific breakthrough or existential threat seems to make the world more aware and more distrusting of an AI ...
altman:iKFqJOSWHTE.desc:
Every day a new scientific breakthrough or existential threat seems to make the world more aware and more distrusting of an AI future that we’re told is rapidly approaching—whether we like it or not. And nobody is more recognized as the face of artificial intelligence—as a technology, an industry, and a civilizational shift—than Open AI founder and CEO Sam Altman. Long before he became a household name, Altman established a towering reputation in Silicon Valley: persuasive prodigy, visionary futurist, relentless CEO. But as OpenAI’s influence broke out of tech’s insular bubble, some of the very same traits that served him well in Northern California have become his greatest liabilities. In a far-ranging conversation taped in San Francisco on September 11th – the first of two sitdowns with Vanity Fair’s Mark Guiducci –  Altman discusses his views on ChatGPT and suicide prevention, safety breaches, and the film ‘Artificial,’ in which Andrew Garfield plays him—along with much more.  “I understand the instinct to say, ‘I don't want the change, I don't want the risk. Just stop it,’” Altman says. “I really hope that hundreds of years from now people look back at our lives and just can't believe how bad we had it.”

This is the first installment of a two-part interview with Altman. You can find the second installment on YouTube and podcast apps now. 

Listen to and follow Fair Game from Vanity Fair on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

Director of Photography: David Topete

altman:mJSnn0GZmls.title: The Power and Responsibility of Sam Altman
altman:mJSnn0GZmls.snippet: This week, Laurie Segall sits down exclusively with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for his first interview since shutting down the ...
altman:mJSnn0GZmls.desc:
This week, Laurie Segall sits down exclusively with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for his first interview since shutting down the Disney-partnered Sora and making the Department of War deal. From power to parenthood, tech addiction and AI acceleration, Laurie interviews Altman about AI’s human impact and the weight of OpenAI’s influence. In a wide ranging interview, Altman describes a near-term future where automated AI researchers could compress a decade of scientific discovery into a single year, fundamentally reshaping society and an era of AI abundance, where solo-founders can build billion-dollar companies with AI agents. But that innovation sits against a complex backdrop with fundamental human questions at stake. Altman addresses concerns over AI-related job loss and reveals what he thinks are AI-proof jobs. Altman, who is also a father, discusses parenting in the age of AI, when he plans to introduce his own product to his child, and how he believes AI could benefit kids in the long run. This is a  conversation with Sam Altman you're not going to hear anywhere else, where the tech titan answers some fundamental questions about control, innovation, consequences, and the world we'll leave behind for our children. 

If you have thoughts or questions for Laurie about this episode or anything Mostly Human, email us at hello@mostlyhuman.com

sundar:B-qch6KMT5s.title: Can Frontier AI Ever Become a Defensible Business?
sundar:B-qch6KMT5s.snippet: Alex finally got Google CEO Sundar Pichai on his podcast, and asked him why anyone needs the AI frontier. But if Google, OpenAI ...
sundar:B-qch6KMT5s.desc:
Alex finally got Google CEO Sundar Pichai on his podcast, and asked him why anyone needs the AI frontier. But if Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta all reach superintelligence, does anyone win? Or do we just end up in a price war for superintelligence?

Journalist Alex Kantrowitz and investor Sheel Mohnot unpack Sundar’s case for frontier AI, from getting an early look at new capabilities to recursive self-improvement. They debate whether there are any moats left in the model business. Then Alex shares Sundar’s revealing answer to the show’s favorite question: why doesn’t AI search work in Gmail? It points to Google’s real bet, a single AI agent that works across all of its apps.

Then, OpenAI’s models come to Google Cloud, now the fastest-growing major cloud at 82% growth. SpaceX reports 161% revenue growth as Elon Musk floats a merger with Tesla. And after Anthropic commits 5% of its equity to a public benefit fund, Musk says he’ll give one SpaceX share to every child in America. Is that generosity, or a way to create a new generation of shareholders?

Plus: Alex’s Threads conspiracy theory runs into real data, and Sheel explains why he bought an onion future that may or may not be legal.

zuck:gGQbkp7S5MM.desc:
Comedian Josh Berry teams up with tech founders Lukas Feddern and Toby Mather for a new podcast asking the one question that really matters: would you actually want to go for a pint with them?

Whether you’re putting away three Guinnesses or none, the real question is whether you’d want them there at all. Expect no discussion whatsoever of AI, DPI or how Triple-Triple-Double is dead. In an industry taking itself ever more seriously, sometimes the only metric that matters is whether you’d enjoy a beer with someone.

We kick things off with Meta/Facebook/Oculus/Instagram/WhatsApp/Roman Empire CEO Mark Zuckerberg, the man who turned Facebook into a global phenomenon, shaped the world of social media and now has turned his ambitions to AI.

New episodes coming soon. 🍺

Welcome back to Impact Theory. Today's episode focused on Tom’s in-depth reactions to two compelling video interviews: one between Walter Isaacson and Elon Musk, the other featuring an OpenAI whistleblower. A key theme that emerged was the unprecedented pace and scope of AI development, captured through Elon Musk’s candid concerns about existential risks and the complexity of shaping artificial intelligence for humanity’s benefit. The discussion explored Musk’s evolving perspective—from early efforts to slow down AI out of safety concerns to an acceptance that he could only participate and attempt to guide its trajectory.

Tom’s analysis didn’t stop there. The second video brought a whistleblower’s insider viewpoint, highlighting unsettling practices and power-seeking incentives within the AI industry, particularly at OpenAI. Several points were raised, including the tension between commercial ambition and societal good, the risks of regulatory capture, and the global race for AI supremacy. The conversation delved into scenarios of automation, economic disruption, and the challenge of maintaining AI as a tool rather than allowing it to become autonomous

Oracle on Tuesday announced an expanded collaboration with OpenAI that brings the artificial intelligence lab's ChatGPT and Codex into the software maker's applications to make databases more actionable.

Mahesh Thiagarajan, Oracle's president of Cloud Infrastructure, told CNBC at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas that using ChatGPT "allows anybody to build an application, deploy it, manage it."

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman joins Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk on stage for an Oracle AI World keynote on Tuesday.
